newsitem.title: UK: Nuclear waste flights spark outrage in Britain.
newsitem.headline: Nuclear waste flights spark outrage in Britain.

text.p: Environmentalists urged Britain on Monday to ban the transport of nuclear waste by air and warned that plans by a power company to fly radioactive materials over cities could endanger the lives of millions of people.

Friends of the Earth criticised a proposal by British Nuclear Fuels (BNFL) to transport plutonium waste from Europe and Japan to its British plant and said it had written to Prime Minister Tony Blair demanding a rethink of the country's nuclear power policy.

"We are horrified to learn that the nuclear industry is planning to fly highly radioactive waste into its new recycling plant at Sellafield," Dr Patrick Green of the environmental group said in a statement.
"If an accident were to happen the consequences would be devastating. The government must act immediately to ban these flights," he added.

News of the proposed flights sparked an uproar in Britain and Labour's new transport minister, Gavin Strang, agreed to an urgent meeting with member of parliament Denis MacShane, whose constituency would be most affected by the flights.
"These flights of death are a potential hazards to towns and villages across the country," MacShane told reporters.
Friends of the Earth claimed BNFL was considering the air transport because it wanted to avoid demonstrations likely to obstruct the route if it is shipped by rail, road or sea.
The group also called for an immediate halt to BNFL's plans to manufacture plutonium-based fuel at its new recycling plant in Cumbria, northern England, from next year.

"If this new plutonium recycling plant is allowed to start operating, it will lead to a major increase in the transportation of plutonium around the UK. This is totally unacceptable," Green said, adding that the population should no longer be exposed to such risks.

BNFL acknowledged that it was considering flying the materials and had already done a test flight, but added that it was only one of four transport options. It also denied that it posed a danger to the population.
"All these materials have to be handled in the proper manner," said John Barbour, media relations manager at the Sellafield plant.

The company said the material would be shipped in special flasks capable of withstanding an air crash. Barbour said that even if, in the remotest circumstances, the package did break open the products have a very low dispersablility.
But the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament rejected the argument.
"The plutonium containers simply could not withstand any serious accident, never mind an air crash," the CND said.
"Any accident would scatter plutonium for hundreds of square kilometres (miles) and vast areas of land would be uninhabitable for thousands of years to come," it added.
Barbour insisted the uproar was a storm in a teacup.
"BNFL has been transporting nuclear materials around the world for many, many years, covering many millions of miles," he said.

"As I understand these types of materials have been moving around for about 30 years, from suppliers to customers. To my knowledge there has never been an accident involving the release of radioactivity."
